---
title: Herbal teas and infusions
lang: en
free: true
---

Herbal teas — more accurately called tisanes — contain no leaves from the tea plant at all. They are infusions of dried flowers, roots, berries, and herbs, which means the rules that apply to true teas do not always transfer.

## Water temperature

Most tisanes tolerate, and often need, fully boiling water. The plant material is tougher than a tea leaf: roots and bark need sustained heat to give up their compounds, and dried flowers like chamomile release their fragrance best when the water is at a rolling boil. The main exception is delicate petals or fresh herbs, which can scorch slightly if the water is too aggressive — letting the kettle cool for a minute is usually enough.

## Steeping

Unlike true teas, tisanes rarely suffer from over-steeping. Most are better left for five to ten minutes rather than pulled early. Chamomile and linden become more soothing with a longer infusion; mint stays bright and fresh for at least five minutes. There is no real risk of bitterness from tannins because most tisanes contain none. Taste at five minutes and decide whether to go longer. A covered cup or teapot retains heat and speeds up the process without requiring more leaf.
